title: Looping Rover Commands
statement:
A rover starts at (0, 0) on an endless flat plane, facing north. It reads a command string made of three letters:

  • 'G': drive forward one unit in the current direction.
  • 'L': turn 90° to the left without moving.
  • 'R': turn 90° to the right without moving.

When it reaches the end of the string it starts again from the first letter, forever. Return true if the rover never leaves some fixed circle around the origin, or false if it drifts away without limit.

examples.why: One pass ends at (2, 2) facing south. The second pass is the first one turned 180°, so it walks back to (0, 0).
One pass moves the rover by (1, 1) and leaves it facing north again, so every pass adds another (1, 1).
It comes back to the origin after one pass. Facing a new direction does not matter then.

hints: Run the commands once and look only at where the rover ends up and which way it faces.
If it faces north again after one pass, every pass adds the same displacement. When is that displacement harmless?
Bounded exactly when, after one pass, it is back at the origin or it no longer faces north. A turned rover undoes its own drift within four passes.

explain.intuition:
Everything a pass does is a move by some vector, followed by a rotation. If after one pass the rover still faces north, the next pass adds exactly the same vector again. It stays near home only if that vector is zero.

If it faces a different way, the next pass is the same path rotated. Rotated by 180°, two passes cancel. Rotated by 90°, four passes add up to the vector rotated through all four directions, which also sums to zero. Either way the rover is back at the origin after at most four passes, so it can never escape.
steps: Keep a position (x, y) and a direction index into [(0,1), (1,0), (0,−1), (−1,0)] (north, east, south, west).
For 'G' add the current direction vector; for 'R' add 1 to the index; for 'L' add 3, all modulo 4.
After one pass, return true if (x, y) = (0, 0) or the direction index is not 0.
pitfalls: Checking only for a return to the origin. In the first example the rover is far away after one pass and still bounded.
Getting left and right backwards in the direction table. That swaps which way the rover goes but not the answer, so it hides in tests; keep the table in clockwise order.
Doing (dir − 1) % 4 in JavaScript: it gives −1. Add 3 instead.

solutions.title: Simulate four passes
solutions.idea: After four passes the rover faces its starting direction whatever the rotation was. It is bounded exactly when it is back at the origin then.

solutions.title: One pass, check position or heading
solutions.idea: Run once. Bounded if the rover is home, or if it no longer faces north (then its drift cancels within four passes).

followups: Return the radius of the smallest circle centred at the origin that contains the whole path, or −1 if it is unbounded.
Add a 'B' command that turns 180°. Does the rule change?
